pointers.sentence: `AuthConfig.ready` connects both receivers to `post_migrate` with no sender, so each runs for every application with a models module, and registers the check among the model checks (`django/contrib/auth/apps.py:AuthConfig.ready`).

`Options.default_permissions` is a tuple of actions, add, change, delete and view unless the `Meta` sets another (`django/db/models/options.py:Options.__init__`); `Options.permissions` is a list of pairs of codename and name, empty unless the `Meta` sets one ([The options: what a model keeps as `_meta`](../models/options.md)).

The codename is the action and the model's name joined by an underscore, `"change_ship"`, made by `get_permission_codename`, which the admin also uses ([Permissions in the admin: `has_change_permission` and the others](../admin/admin-permissions.md)) (`django/contrib/auth/__init__.py:get_permission_codename`).
The name is "Can", the action and `Options.verbose_name_raw`, the verbose name untranslated whatever language is active (`django/contrib/auth/management/__init__.py:_get_builtin_permissions`).
`_get_all_permissions` puts the `Meta`'s own pairs after these (`django/contrib/auth/management/__init__.py:_get_all_permissions`).

`create_permissions` returns without a write when the application has no models module; when the registry it is given has no `Permission` (auth not installed, or its migrations not applied in the state); when the router does not let `Permission` be migrated on the database it is given; or when the registry has no `ContentType` or no such application (`django/contrib/auth/management/__init__.py:create_permissions`).

Otherwise it first calls `create_contenttypes` for the application, which clears `ContentTypeManager`'s cache and makes the missing content types (`django/contrib/contenttypes/management/__init__.py:create_contenttypes`).

It takes the application's models from the registry, less the models made for many-to-many fields and those swapped out (`django/apps/config.py:AppConfig.get_models`), and their content types from `ContentTypeManager.get_for_models` with `for_concrete_models=False`, which gives a proxy its own content type, and so its own permissions, and makes any it does not find.

The registry being a state's, a permission added to a `Meta` in an application with migrations is made by the migrate that applies the `AlterModelOptions` recording it (`django/db/migrations/operations/models.py:AlterModelOptions`); the models of an application without migrations are rendered from their classes.

Tug's rows are under office, so nora's `"fleet.change_ship"` gives nothing over tugs: a proxy does not inherit its concrete model's permissions, as Django's documentation puts it (`docs/topics/auth/default.txt`).
Without a plan, as from flush, it does nothing (`django/contrib/auth/management/__init__.py:rename_permissions_after_model_rename`).

For each rename it reads the model's actions and verbose name from the registry, or, for a model the state no longer has, `Permission`'s default actions and the model's name (`django/contrib/auth/management/__init__.py:_get_permission_metadata`).
A permission's name and codename are renamed when a migration renames its model (`docs/releases/6.1.txt`).

Where the proxy already has such a row the update raises `IntegrityError`, and the migration prints a warning naming both content types and goes on (`django/contrib/auth/migrations/0011_update_proxy_permissions.py:update_proxy_model_permissions`).
The release notes of 2.2, which changed that, give this migration as the way existing rows follow (`docs/releases/2.2.txt`).

It reports a built-in name or codename too long, with the longest verbose name or model name that would fit (`"auth.E007"`, `"auth.E011"`); a `Meta` pair whose name or codename is too long (`"auth.E008"`, `"auth.E012"`); a `Meta` codename that is also a built-in one (`"auth.E005"`); and any other `Meta` codename given twice (`"auth.E006"`) (`django/contrib/auth/checks.py:check_models_permissions`).
